clue.text: Sometimes seen hanging around at the back in church

definitions.text: Sometimes seen hanging around at the back in church

parts.words: Sometimes seen hanging around at the back in church
parts.note: describes an ornamental cloth hung behind the altar of a church, sometimes spelt with an R and so 'at the back' in the sense of dorsal

explanation.surface: A loiterer who lurks at the back of a church during services.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hanging around' suggests a person idling, but it is a literal hanging cloth; 'at the back' nods to the variant spelling dorsal, meaning of the back.
explanation.definitionFit: A dossal is an embroidered curtain or cloth hung behind an altar, so it is seen hanging at the back of a church.

clue.text: Bernard Capes's knight errant gets healing ointment

definitions.meaning: a character, ..., in a romance by the Edwardian writer Bernard Capes
the balm of ..., a soothing resin named after the biblical region

explanation.surface: A wandering knight from an old romance is given a salve for his wounds.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is a fictional character's name; the other is short for the balm of the biblical region, a proverbial healing salve.

clue.text: Badly hampering a loyal follower of Henry V

definitions.text: a loyal follower of Henry V

indicators.note: something done badly is botched or mangled, so the following word's letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone loyal to the king nonetheless gets in his way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Badly' rearranges HAMPERING. Sir Thomas Erpingham is the old knight who lends King Henry his cloak before Agincourt in Shakespeare's play.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Erpingham was a historical knight who served Henry V at Agincourt and appears as a faithful old soldier in Shakespeare's history play.

clue.text: Stravinsky piece describing gymnastic ceremony?

definitions.meaning: the 1913 ballet score by Igor Stravinsky that caused a riot at its Paris premiere
a ritual (rite) performed with springing leaps, read as a phrase

explanation.surface: A piece of music is said to depict athletes performing a ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the whimsical second reading: a rite made of springs, the bouncing kind gymnasts do.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballet's title is literally a ceremony (rite) of leaping (spring), so the phrase also describes a gymnastic ritual.

clue.text: Possibly Ibsen's Ghosts from Southern underworld

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for south or southern
Hades is the Greek underworld, realm of the dead

explanation.surface: A suggestion that the spirits in Ibsen's play came up from the underworld below.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ghosts' is the title of an Ibsen play, but here it simply means spirits of the dead; 'Possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: Shades are spirits of the dead, so the ghosts of the play's title could be described this way.

clue.text: Bust up in Athenian violence

clue.text: His second opinion was not much valued

definitions.text: His second opinion was not much valued

parts.words: His second opinion was not much valued
parts.note: a medical man whose view, as second fiddle to Sherlock Holmes, was seldom heeded by his friend

explanation.surface: A doctor's second opinion counted for little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second opinion' sounds like a medical consultation; it means the opinion of the sidekick, always second to the great detective's.
explanation.definitionFit: Holmes's companion was a physician whose deductions were routinely overruled by the detective, so his opinion came second and was little prized.

clue.text: Eminent Victorian chronicler

parts.note: points to the 1918 book of four irreverent biographies, Eminent Victorians, by a Bloomsbury writer

explanation.surface: A distinguished nineteenth-century historian.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a famous Victorian who wrote chronicles; in fact the writer was the twentieth-century author of the book 'Eminent Victorians'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lytton Strachey wrote the debunking biographical collection Eminent Victorians, chronicling Manning, Nightingale, Arnold and Gordon.

clue.text: "I never saw a wild thing/ sorry for itself" (-—, D. H. Lawrence)

definitions.text: "I never saw a wild thing/ sorry for itself" (-—, D. H. Lawrence)

parts.words: "I never saw a wild thing/ sorry for itself" (-—, D. H. Lawrence)
parts.note: the opening lines of a short poem by D. H. Lawrence, whose title the dash asks the solver to supply

explanation.surface: A quotation from a Lawrence poem with its title left blank.
explanation.walkthrough: The poem's title names exactly what wild creatures never feel: sorrow for themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's title is the emotion the lines describe animals as lacking, feeling sorry for oneself.

clue.text: Lexicographer who may have agreed that "Malt does more than Milton can…"

definitions.meaning: E. Cobham ..., compiler of the Dictionary of Phrase and Fable

definitions.text: who may have agreed that "Malt does more than Milton can…"
definitions.meaning: a maker of beer from malt, who would endorse A. E. Housman's line praising ale over Paradise Lost

explanation.surface: A dictionary-maker who might have backed Housman's praise of ale over poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Housman's line in A Shropshire Lad continues 'To justify God's ways to man', setting beer against Milton; a beer-maker would naturally agree.
explanation.definitionFit: Ebenezer Cobham Brewer compiled a famous dictionary, and a beer-maker who works with malt shares the surname as a trade.

clue.text: Hardly recognizable in lock-in gaol in Hume Nisbet's creation

indicators.note: something hardly recognizable has been transformed, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: A prisoner after a pub lock-in is barely recognisable in a jail cell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardly recognizable' rearranges LOCK-IN GAOL IN. Hume Nisbet was a Scottish-Australian novelist of the 1890s.
explanation.definitionFit: A Colonial King is a novel by the writer Hume Nisbet, so it is one of his literary creations.

clue.text: Like a secondhand signature on a sitcom rewrite

indicators.note: a rewrite reworks a script, so the preceding letters are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A script rewrite of a sitcom borrows an autograph from someone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rewrite' rearranges ON A SITCOM. A secondhand signature here is one written by another person on someone's behalf.
explanation.definitionFit: Onomastic, relating to names, describes a signature in another hand where only the name, not the text, is written by the signer.

clue.text: Anser Caerulescens as. Henry Prize winner

definitions.meaning: the Latin name of a white North American wild goose
Paul Gallico's novella won the O. Henry Award for short fiction in 1941

explanation.surface: A bird's Latin name sits beside a literary award winner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin binomial names that white Arctic goose, and Gallico's story of the same title took the O. Henry award for short fiction.

clue.text: Keys Roget might provide for jungle lord

indicators.note: the letters might provide something new once they are reordered, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A thesaurus could supply the key words for a Tarzan story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Might provide' rearranges KEYS ROGET. Tarzan is the heir to the title Lord Greystoke in Edgar Rice Burroughs's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Tarzan of the Apes is by birth John Clayton, Lord Greystoke, the noble ruler of the jungle.

clue.text: Munitions worker and collaborator produced dramatic results

definitions.meaning: a maker of arrows, the munitions of archery
John ..., the Jacobean playwright who co-wrote with Beaumont and with Shakespeare

explanation.surface: An arms-factory hand and a partner who produced spectacular results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Munitions' suggests shells and bullets; an arrow-maker supplied the munitions of the longbow age. 'Dramatic' is literal: his collaborations were plays.
explanation.definitionFit: An arrow-maker supplies weapons, and the Jacobean dramatist co-authored plays with Francis Beaumont.

clue.text: Newbolt's were all in verse

parts.note: points to the patriotic naval poem by Sir Henry Newbolt whose title pairs these sea commanders with the word all

explanation.surface: Everything Newbolt wrote was poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a remark about Newbolt's output; it alludes to his poem 'Admirals All', where the commanders are 'all' and in verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Newbolt's ballad 'Admirals All' celebrates Drake, Nelson and other naval commanders, so his fleet chiefs were all set in verse.

clue.text: When she was about to sing in Welsh, Percy said he would sooner hear his dog howl in Irish

definitions.text: When she was about to sing in Welsh, Percy said he would sooner hear his dog howl in Irish

parts.words: When she was about to sing in Welsh, Percy said he would sooner hear his dog howl in Irish
parts.note: recalls the scene in Henry IV Part 1 where Glendower's daughter, married to an English lord, sings in Welsh and Hotspur mocks it

explanation.surface: A singer about to perform in Welsh is rudely heckled by Percy.
explanation.walkthrough: Percy is Hotspur, who tells his wife he would rather hear his brach (hound) howl in Irish than listen to the Welsh song.
explanation.definitionFit: Glendower's Welsh-speaking daughter, wife of Edmund Mortimer, sings to her husband in Shakespeare's history play while Hotspur jeers.

clue.text: Italians in French fiction

definitions.meaning: people of Rome, the Italian capital

explanation.surface: Italians appearing in French novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the Italian capital share the spelling of the French plural for novels.

clue.text: Sassoon traced its journey

parts.note: alludes to the 1928 collection of poems by Siegfried Sassoon whose title is the journey of an organ of feeling

explanation.surface: Siegfried Sassoon mapped out a route.
explanation.walkthrough: Sassoon's volume 'The Heart's Journey' gives the answer with its apostrophe: the journey belongs to the organ of feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: Siegfried Sassoon's poetry collection The Heart's Journey traces the travels of the seat of emotion.

clue.text: Instructive form of a Loti unit

indicators.note: a different form of the following letters is made by reordering them

explanation.surface: A section of a Pierre Loti novel turns out to be educational.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Form of' rearranges A LOTI UNIT. Pierre Loti was a French naval officer and novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: Relating to teaching or tutoring, so instructive in character.

clue.text: Those revering saltire necessarily including MacDonald's princess

indicators.note: the run of words is said to include the answer, so its letters sit inside them

explanation.surface: Scots who honour the St Andrew's cross must take in a fairy-tale princess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Including' points to IRENE, which runs across the join of 'saltIRE NEcessarily'. George MacDonald's The Princess and the Goblin has Princess Irene as its heroine.
explanation.definitionFit: Irene is the young royal heroine of George MacDonald's fantasy The Princess and the Goblin.

clue.text: Was he inclined to be Dr Proudie's chaplain?

definitions.text: Was he inclined to be Dr Proudie's chaplain?

parts.words: Was he inclined to be Dr Proudie's chaplain?
parts.note: the bishop's oily chaplain in Trollope's Barchester Towers, whose surname also means an incline

explanation.surface: A question about whether a clergyman wanted the post of bishop's chaplain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inclined' seems to mean willing; it also means sloping, which is the surname of Obadiah, chaplain to Bishop Proudie in Trollope.
explanation.definitionFit: Obadiah Slope is Bishop Proudie's scheming chaplain in Barchester Towers, and his surname means a sloping incline.

clue.text: It was Wilder's goal

parts.note: alludes to Thornton Wilder's 1935 novel whose title names the paradise that is the hero's destination

explanation.surface: A remark about what an ambitious person was aiming for.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wilder' looks like a comparative of wild; it is Thornton Wilder, author of 'Heaven's My Destination'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wilder's novel Heaven's My Destination names paradise as the hero's journey's end, so it is the stated goal.

clue.text: Junior has consumed Greek tea, say? that's a lot of bull

indicators.note: the first word swallows the second, so its letters go inside

parts.note: junior means minor, lesser in rank or age
tau is the Greek letter T, whose name 'tea' sounds like

explanation.surface: A youngster has drunk some Greek tea, which sounds like nonsense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Junior' reads as a youngster drinking tea, and 'a lot of bull' as slang for nonsense; in fact the monster of Crete was half bull, and the Greek letter is named for its sound.
explanation.definitionFit: The Minotaur of Cretan myth had a bull's head on a man's body, so much of it was bovine.

clue.text: An apple for W. W. Jacobs's seaman

definitions.meaning: a rough-skinned brownish variety of eating apple
a sailor character in the comic sea stories of W. W. Jacobs

explanation.surface: An apple handed to a sailor from a Jacobs story.
explanation.definitionFit: The name is both a brownish dessert apple variety and the surname of a seafaring character in W. W. Jacobs's tales.

clue.text: Advances made by upfront PR for man-eaters

indicators.note: the advances are made by placing the letters PR upfront, so taking them off the front leaves the remainder

parts.note: taken as written, the initials of public relations

explanation.surface: Aggressive public-relations work makes advances on predatory people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made by upfront PR' says PROGRESSES is PR plus the rest, so removing PR leaves the answer. 'Man-eaters' sounds like predatory women; it is literal for these monsters.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogresses are female giants of folklore who devour humans.
